title: Campaigns spend big to sway voters with increasingly personal attack ads
summary: Lisa Desjardins reports on a record-breaking final-week wave of midterm ads, most of them centred on the cost of living, with Republicans and outside groups outspending rivals though the gap is closing. Analysts from AdImpact and the Wesleyan Media Project explain how President Trump largely vanished from GOP ads, how personal attacks such as an Ohio ad featuring a candidate's estranged mother are blending with policy contrasts, and how AI-generated ads are spreading. Despite voters saying they find the barrage distasteful, the experts argue the sustained spending shows campaigns believe the ads move votes.
focus: Shadow Fowler's explanation of why issue-based negative ads can be legitimate but are now blurring into personal attacks, and Link's short closing argument that persistent spending proves campaigns think ads work — both are clear, analytical and evenly paced.

vocab.meaning: how far people can pay for things such as housing, food and energy
vocab.context: Named as the central theme that ads from both parties keep returning to.
vocab.example: Our survey shows affordability, not brand loyalty, is now the main driver of churn in the mid-market segment.

vocab.meaning: to count up and record a running total
vocab.context: Describes how an ad-tracking firm adds up the money spent on political advertising.
vocab.example: Once finance tallies the one-off costs, we will know whether the integration actually broke even.

vocab.meaning: to spend more money than a rival
vocab.context: Used to compare how much more one party and outside groups were spending than their opponents.
vocab.example: The challenger brand cannot outspend the incumbent, so it has to out-target it.

vocab.meaning: (of a gap or difference) to become smaller
vocab.context: Explains how the spending gap between the parties shrank as Election Day approached.
vocab.example: The margin gap with our closest competitor narrowed to two points after their cost programme.

vocab.meaning: higher or larger than anything achieved before
vocab.context: Describes the unprecedented volume of political ads in this midterm cycle.
vocab.example: The firm posted record-breaking bookings in Q3, but much of it was pulled forward from Q4.

vocab.meaning: taking unfair advantage of a person or situation for one's own gain
vocab.context: A candidate used it to condemn an ad that featured her estranged relative.
vocab.example: The board rejected the pricing model as exploitative of customers locked into long contracts.

vocab.meaning: to criticise someone very strongly and publicly
vocab.context: Used for relatives of victims harshly criticising lawmakers in an ad.
vocab.example: Activist investors blasted management for sitting on cash instead of returning it to shareholders.

vocab.example: Our risk review flagged deepfakes of executives as a growing threat to investor communications.

vocab.meaning: to become closely connected or twisted together

phrases.meaning: to repeat a point forcefully so that people fully understand it
phrases.context: Describes how one party kept pressing its cost-of-living message in ad after ad.
phrases.example: In the steering committee, hammer home the one number that matters: payback in 18 months.

phrases.meaning: to keep going financially and avoid failure or debt
phrases.zh: 维持生计；勉强维持（不倒闭）
phrases.context: Used for families struggling with grocery and fuel bills that ads appealed to.
phrases.example: Several regional carriers are only staying afloat thanks to short-term credit lines.

phrases.meaning: to keep supporting a decision or person despite criticism
phrases.context: Describes a campaign that kept defending its controversial ad despite bipartisan backlash.
phrases.example: The CEO stuck by the restructuring plan even after the share price dipped.

phrases.meaning: to try to match what your peers or rivals are doing or spending
phrases.context: An ad-tracking expert rejected the idea that campaigns spend just to match each other, arguing they believe the ads work.
phrases.example: Don't build a metaverse unit just to keep up with the Joneses; tie it to a customer need.

phrases.meaning: seen as too lenient towards criminals
phrases.context: Cited as a common attack line campaigns use against opponents.
phrases.example: In policy-sensitive markets, being labelled soft on compliance can hurt a bank more than any fine.
